title: 3-Read Friday #22: The Hypercorrection Effect, Textbook Design, and Praising Your Team
author: Craig Barton
summary: Issue 22 of 3-Read Friday gathers three posts spanning cognitive science, resource design, and leadership. Barton leads with the InnerDrive team's deep dive into the Hypercorrection Effect, describing his own fascination with the phenomenon where confidently-held wrong answers become more memorable once corrected, and valuing the piece for pairing the research with classroom-ready suggestions. His second pick, Michael Pershan's "Textbooks Don't Have to Be This Bad," gets framed as an extension of Pershan's book Teaching Math with Examples into general textbook and resource design, which Barton argues has relevance well beyond maths specifically. His third selection, Ian Frost's ten-point piece on praising staff well, is explicitly reframed from its leadership audience to apply to all teachers, on the grounds that the underlying principles of specific, unblurred, well-timed praise work in peer and student relationships too. As with most issues, Barton's own commentary is brief and appreciative rather than argumentative, functioning as a curated pointer to three pieces he personally found valuable that week.
points: Barton frames the Hypercorrection Effect pick around his own enthusiasm for the phenomenon, signalling personal investment in cognitive-science content rather than neutral curation.

He connects Michael Pershan's textbook-design piece explicitly back to Pershan's book Teaching Math with Examples, positioning the blog post as a distilled, more broadly applicable version of the book's argument.

Barton extends Ian Frost's leadership-focused praise piece to all teachers, arguing the principles for delivering praise well transfer beyond headteacher-staff dynamics into peer and student interactions.
The issue's three picks span cognitive science, materials design, and interpersonal leadership skill - a deliberately wide net typical of the format rather than a single unifying theme.
quotes: I am obsessed with the Hypercorrection Effect - the phenomenon where when we are both wrong and confident about something, and then get corrected through feedback, we are more likely to remember the right information.
The InnerDrive team takes a deep dive into the Hypercorrection Effect, along with practical suggestions of how its power can be harnessed in the classroom.
Michael applies the thinking behind his fantastic book, Teaching Math with Examples, to the subject of textbook design.
The principles Michael discusses here are relevant to anyone designing any form of learning materials, from worksheets to PowerPoints.
Ian delves into the concept of praise, sharing ten practical strategies that can make praise more effective.
Whilst aimed at leaders, the ideas discussed here have relevance for all teachers, helping improve their interactions with both their colleagues and their students.
